subsubtopic: INCLUSION OF GRATUITIES AS WAGES IN CALCULATING UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFITS
speechtext: Can waiters and waitresses include gratuities as wages in calculating unemployment benefits in the same manner as for income tax purposes and, if not, for what reason?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Stanbury (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: INCLUSION OF GRATUITIES AS WAGES IN CALCULATING UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFITS
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of National Revenue, Taxa-

tion, is concerned: Gratuities received by waiters and waitresses directly from the customer are not included in insurable earnings for purposes of calculating unemployment insurance benefits. The legislation provides that premiums are to be deducted only if the remuneration is paid by the employer. Further to this, the employer does not know the amount of gratuities received by each employee. Where an employer includes a service charge in the billing to the customer and in turn passes this service charge on to the employees, he is required to deduct employees' premiums and pay employer's premiums with regard to gratuities that are paid in this manner. These gratuities would then constitute insurable earnings.

MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 TRADE STATE OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES ON AUTO PACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move a motion for the adjournment of the House pursu-
February 28, 1973

ant to Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the state of negotiations between Canada and the United States with respect to the Canada-U.S. auto pact, in view of recent statements by the vice-president of General Motors Corporation and officials of the United States Treasury Department concerning a $100 million trade deficit for Canada and particularly the proposed continuing insistence by the United States on the removal of the present Canadian safeguards.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 TRADE STATE OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH UNITED STATES ON AUTO PACT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Halton has forwarded the notice required under Standing Order 26 and I have had an opportunity to consider the several aspects of the proposed motion.
The precedents, as well as the Standing Order itself, provide that in ruling whether the business of the House ought to be set aside for an emergency debate the Chair should take into account a number of factors, including the opportunity for debate within a reasonable time. In the present circumstances it would be difficult for the Chair to ignore the fact that the House is now engaged in the budget debate. A long established practice indicates that the budget debate, as well as the throne speech debate, are both deemed to provide the type of opportunity for debate envisaged and contemplated by Standing Order 26. There are many rulings to this effect.
While I recognize the interest and concern of all hon. members in this urgent question, I have concluded that there are in fact, or will be, a number of opportunities for debate within a reasonable time, one of these being the budget debate which is to be called under government orders later this day. It is with regret that I have to reach this conclusion and make this ruling in the hope that the hon. member for Halton, who has proposed this debate under the terms of Standing Order 26, will have the opportunity during the budget debate or other opportunities within the next few days to bring this matter to the attention of the House, to make his representations and to institute a debate.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. With reference to the indication yesterday that our automobile and automotive parts trade position with the United States amounted to a $100 million deficit in 1972, will the minister advise the House of the reasons for such a deficit occurring and, further, whether this deficit is a temporary reversal or the beginning of a future trend?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Statistics Canada today published the figure. The figure is not $100 million; it is a $41 million deficit on the merchandise trade account. This reverses the position of last year when, according to our figures, we had a surplus on merchandise account of just under $200 million. I would expect with the auto pact that there would be shifts in trade balance figures from time to time. I do not see that there is any emergency or any reason to push any panic button at this time.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: In view of the fact there has been a transition from a $200 million surplus to a $41 million or $100 million deficit, as the case may be, is the minister satisfied that the production to sales ratio and the Canadian value-added safeguards contained in the auto pact were strictly adhered to by all auto manufacturers operating in Canada in 1972?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: I should like to take this opportunity to say I believe there is a lot of misunderstanding with respect to the so-called safeguards. They were transitional measures introduced at the start of the auto pact, and at present levels we are exceeding the levels of those transitional provisions by $1 billion or more.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: With respect, the minister has failed to answer my question. Is he satisfied that all manufacturers and parts manufacturers in Canada have strictly adhered to these safeguards as set out in the auto pact?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: As I have pointed out, by at least a billion dollars.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
Was the production and employment percentage of the total North American Market reduced from the levels achieved in 1971? Further, what steps is the
Oral Questions
government taking to ensure that these critical levels will not be substantially altered in the future?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: With respect to production-employment ratios, I would have to check. I will be pleased to do so and report back to the hon. member.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Will the minister insist, in his negotiations with the United States, that Canadians have the opportunity to buy cars made in Canada at the same price as Americans pay for Canadian cars?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: As hon. members will recall, one of the first tasks I took on as Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, was to narrow the gap between the wholesale price of vehicles made in Canada and those made in the United States. I received an undertaking from the automobile manufacturers in Canada that if there is any increase in prices in the United States there will be no increase in Canada. To the extent that there is an increase in the United States, the gap will then be narrowed. At the time I received this commitment the United States companies were pursuing an application for a 3 per cent increase.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: We are not asking for the gap to be narrowed. We are asking for exactly the same price.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: My supplementary refers to the answer the minister gave a minute or so ago. This is the first time to my knowledge that any minister of the Crown has publicly acknowledged that the government regards the safeguards as being transitional. Would the minister make it clear now that the government regards the safeguards in the Canada-United States automobile agreement as being transitional only?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: I think it has been made clear in the past that the word "safeguard" is not a word used in the agreement itself. The phrase used in the agreement is "transitional provisions". When reference is made to the so-called safeguards I think the hon. member must be referring to the transitional provisions, because I am unaware of any other so-called safeguards in the agreement.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: In view of the fact that in the opening paragraphs of the agreement there is a statement signed by both governments that Canada is to get its fair and equitable share of the production in the North American automotive industry and that this is followed in the agreement by a commitment that the level of production in Canada is not to fall below that achieved in 1964, and in view of the fact that yesterday in the United States treasury officials reasserted their desire to get rid of these aspects of the agreement specifically, as I understand the position, can the minister tell the House whether or not the government of Canada has agreed with that approach?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext:
No discussions have taken place with the United States following the committee hearings to which the hon. member has referred. But let me repeat that the

February 28, 1973
Oral Questions
auto agreement is, in our view, working very successfully. We believe it is working very successfully in the United States, and it is presently operating in Canada at a level of a billion dollars over those transitional provisions.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: The minister is still being evasive. Will he tell the House whether it is the position of the government that the job-protecting requirements relating to production levels in Canada which are written into the agreement should be maintained? Is the government committed to maintaining them or is it prepared to allow them to be taken out of the agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: We are committed to making the auto pact work so that there will be increased employment. That is the important thing, I should like to remind the hon. member. I can see no point at this time in creating baseless fears in the minds of the public with respect to the so-called safeguards.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: We are committed to making the pact work, to building a larger market in North America and a larger share in that market.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, when the minister says there are misunderstandings, he is right. Can he give any explanation for one of the auto companies saying there was a deficit last year of $100 million while according to Statistics Canada there was a deficit of $41 million? What is his department's estimate of the deficit last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: I have already stated that Statistics Canada has published figures today showing that the deficit on merchandise trade flow was $41 million in the past year.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: And I have asked for an explanation of that difference. Can the minister answer that question for me-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Order. Is the hon. member repeating the question he asked in the first instance? If he is, there is not much point in his continuing.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Then I will ask the minister whether any date for new trade talks is now under discussion with the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: No date has been set. I should like to remind the hon. member that I am not the person who puts together the statistics issued by General Motors in the United States. If he wishes to find out the reason for the difference I suggest he call General Motors in the United States.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-REASONS FOR CANADIAN DEFICIT POSITION IN 1972-MAINTENANCE OF SAFEGUARDS
speechtext: Don't you think you should do it?

CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-CANADIAN REACTION TO UNITED STATES POSITION
speechtext:
Does the minister reject the position taken by United States treasury officials that the automotive trade figures last year were

nothing more than an aberration and that the auto pact is actually working to the detriment of United States interests? If he does reject that position, will he tell the House why the government is lagging in its negotiations in connection with this matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-CANADIAN REACTION TO UNITED STATES POSITION
speechtext: I do not think the auto pact is any aberration. I do not think its success as far as Canada is concerned is an aberration at all. Nor do I think that spokesmen in the United States regard it in that way. In fact, one report I read stated that the auto pact had been of very considerable benefit to the United States, too.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-CANADIAN REACTION TO UNITED STATES POSITION
speechtext: I would ask the minister again: does he reject the position taken by the United States and, if so, why has he not begun negotiations with them at an earlier date?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-CANADIAN REACTION TO UNITED STATES POSITION
speechtext: I am not at all clear what particular position the hon. member is imputing to the United States government at this time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-CANADIAN REACTION TO UNITED STATES POSITION
speechtext: Order, please. I will recognize the hon. member for a supplementary and then the hon. member for Waterloo.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-CANADIAN REACTION TO UNITED STATES POSITION
speechtext: United States officials have said that last year's trade figures were a mere aberration and that the auto pact is working to the detriment of the United States. subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES AUTO PACT-CANADIAN REACTION TO UNITED STATES POSITION

subtopic: CATALOGUE ISSUED BY DEPARTMENT-REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF THERAPEUTIC EQUIVALENCY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the QUAD program is one of the steps taken by the government to help reduce the cost to the consumer of drugs in this country. The QUAD program contains three basic elements: one, to establish quality, the chemical testing; two, the evaluation of the manufacturing capabilities; three, the measure of clinical effectiveness. The House resumed, from Tuesday, February 27, consideration of the motion of Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance) that this House approve in general the budgetary policy of the government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I had to interrupt my speech yesterday evening, I should like to point out that another cause of inflation is that collective agreements have these past ten years provided the Canadian workers with annual salary increases of about 5 per cent. Five per cent raises are granted to one sector of the economy one year, and the next year other collective agreements make it necessary to give raises to other sectors, so as to ensure some degree of uniformity in salary
February 28, 1973

scales, and so it goes on and on. In the end, everyone is earning more but no one is getting more buying power.
Not that I am opposed to collective agreements or to unions; on the contrary, I consider that they have done a fine job and have greatly contributed to the workers' welfare. I would, however, suggest that the federal government, the unions and the employers carry out a joint study of this vicious circle, with a view to putting an end to this plethora of raises, which are getting us nowhere and are adding to the inflationary pressures.
The budget also assists small businesses, Mr. Speaker, through elimination of the ineligible investment test as from January 1, 1972. According to the fiscal reform, small Canadian businesses are taxable at the rate of 25 per cent of profits resulting from their operations. However, any investment income was taxable at 50 p. 100. As a result, management of small businesses had adopted a policy of distributing as dividends or otherwise a very substantial part of accumulated profits, resulting in a serious lack of liquid assets in our businesses. A reduction of the tax rate on investment income from 50 to 25 p. 100 therefore encourages small businesses to increase their operating funds in periods of stability and to invest surpluses in bonds, mortgages or other Canadian investments.
In this manner, when those businesses are prepared to expand, they will merely have to liquidate their investments in order to finance development.
This is a measure which will enable our smaller industries to save more; thus, a larger share of our economy will belong to Canadians and no longer to foreign investors.
This budget also introduces a new concept in our tax system, that of including in the calculation of equalization payments the amounts paid in school taxes. Today, most of our Canadian municipalities are faced with a crucial problem. In 1973-74, $190 million will be paid to the Atlantic provinces, Manitoba and Saskatchewan; this amount represents 28 per cent of the school taxes levied in those provinces.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) also increased to $100 the basic old age security pension. I am happy to see that not only the guaranteed income supplement has been increased but also the basic pension because, to my mind, those Canadians who have paid taxes all their lives have the right to that pension; it is not a social security benefit, but their due.
The workers who have contributed to superannuation funds of private companies or other employers are eligible when they retire to a pension at a fixed amount proportional to the amount they have paid, notwithstanding their eventual investment revenues.
The present gap between the basic pension and the guaranteed income supplement must be progressively reduced, because it is unfair to the Canadian worker who, through his work and because of the sacrifices be willingly accepted in order to save money, has often managed to save $10,000 or $15,000 a year throughout his life. Canadians are thus penalized, because in calculating the guaranteed income supplement, the interest gained on saved capital is deducted, which leaves him with a pension
The Budget-Mr. Wagner
altogether equal to that of the taxpayer who never took the trouble to save. Canadians are accordingly encouraged to spend all their earnings, knowing that when they reach 60 or 65 they can live at the expense of the state.
I even think that in the future the gap between the basic pension and the guaranteed income supplement should be further reduced even if the $1,000 tax exemption granted to pensioners has to be abolished.
The suppression of the $1,000 exemption would make the taxation system fairer, so that with an equal revenue, one would pay an equal tax.
This budget is certainly the best in many years, if not since the beginning of Confederation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members have several ways of analyzing the budget now under consideration. One of them is to look at it with the eyes of the head of a family. The more time passes by, the more it seems fair to me to say that it is in terms of its social impact that the budget introduced by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) must be assessed.
The Liberal members and those who are no longer in such a hurry and who are sitting to my left cannot indeed contend decently that this budget is beneficial to the average Canadian family. Looking at it this way would amount to considering the family merely through a statistical prim.
Mr. Speaker, a family is a reality. In the province of Quebec-and I am referring here to the family in Saint-Hyacinthe, as well as the family almost anywhere else in Canada-the family relies more and more on the authorities in search both of a reassessement of its status and life conditions which would not only encourage its complete development, but even constitute its very existence.
It is sad to realize today that our colleagues of the New Democratic Party, the new "democratic paradox", find it normal that the corporate welfare bums should retain what they use to call privileges, and at the same time that the family should gradually lose its rights. Helping out the family meant in particular-and that is what we would have done had we been in office-suppressing the 11 per cent tax on building materials. If I may parody here our Social Credit friends, I would say that we would have thus made financially feasible what is physically possible, namely the desire of every father and mother to have their children educated in a home that would be personal to them and rich in comfort and in intimacy.
Concerning the suppression of the tax on children's clothing and footwear, that is a step forward, but a most bashful one. It is well known, Mr. Speaker, that the 39 cents saved on the one hand on the purchase of footwear for junior will not be enough on the other hand to compensate for the increase, due to inflation, in the price of the maternity dress which the mother has to buy.
And now we know it, Mr. Speaker: a Progressive Conservative government would have removed the federal sales tax on all kinds of clothing and footwear; as for the mascara of the fashionable woman, I couldn't care less!
This, Mr. Speaker, would have really helped the family.

February 28, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Wagner
This budget will not put luxuries within the means of people aged 60 and over. At least 786,000 Canadian citizens between 60 and 65 are being told once more, despite the people's will: "status quo". The government would not even agree to lower the eligible age for retirement. Some 145,000 persons aged 64 across the country are disappointed with the last budget. Yet it is time, Mr. Speaker, to forget about partisanship and to bring gradually into to the federal pension plan all those aged 60.
Even here, "David" did not dare pit himself against the Liberal Goliath. Making a U-turn, he preferred in an anti-historical gesture use his sling against people smaller than him and in some cases against those very people who favoured him at the expense of Goliath.
This budget, Mr. Speaker, is not either that of the Golden Age, nor will it ever come of age, because it was stillborn It was produced by a couple that entered into a friendly agreement which has more to do with political immorality than with the desire to create sound results for the people.
From the social point of view, Mr. Speaker, the budget of the present government is a failure since it ignores the family and minimizes the needs of older people.
From the purely economic point of view, my distinguished colleagues, and I am thinking here of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and the hon. members for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and Don Valley (Mr. Gillies), have shown in this debate the weaknesses of the budget speech of the Minister of Finance.
The rate of increase of the cost of living erodes the increases in salaries or welfare benefits for some and the incentive to work for pay for others and yet the government is still doing nothing more, as the Minister of Finance said, than calling for voluntary restraint as a means to curb inflation.
Earlier, Mr. Speaker, I spoke as a family man, as a Quebecker. I say that no province has more to be bitterly disappointed about in this budget than Quebec. A province whose people have the right to participate in the mainstream of Canadian economic life has been given no meaningful incentive or encouragement to do so in this budget. The pensioner, the workingman and the small businessman in Quebec can, with strong reason, be united in their disappointment.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and members of his cabinet have long prided themselves on the political success their party has had repeatedly in the province of Quebec. As I sit and look across the way at many of my fellow Quebeckers who chose to serve as Liberal members, and when I note the increase in costs and unemployment for Quebeckers under this government, I cannot but rephrase the words of a great parliamentarian of another era and say: Never have so many taken so long to do so little for those they represent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
For while it is all very well for government agencies such as the one formerly headed by the Minister

of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to seek to equalize disparity through regional development grants, the measure of a government's economic success lies in its ability to create a climate in which all citizens can help themselves to achieve a better standard of living.
Those who represent Quebec in this House know full well the type of people we have the honour of speaking for here in Ottawa. Whether a Quebec member sits with the government, the Creditistes or with the official opposition, he or she knows full well that those who sent us here are a self-reliant group of Canadians desirous of neither special economic favours nor handouts. We from Quebec know that Quebeckers want to participate in our nation's economy while standing on their own economic feet-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-as opposed to relying on an election platform artificially propped up by some last minute grants. We from Quebec should ask ourselves what this budget should have done for young Quebeckers leaving CEGEP or college and seeking work, and what it should have done for housewives trying to meet the steadily rising cost of living. After asking these questions, Quebec members who support this budget know full well to what degree they are selling out their constituents' interests.
Mr. Speaker, we are getting closer and closer to the day when those whose interest was sold out on the carving block of parliamentary expediency will vote against those who so willingly made that sale. It may be very easy for government members from Quebec to join their colleagues in making parliamentary deals with the New Democratic paradox, but let them be fully aware that the price of NDP support this week in Ottawa will be paid by Liberal candidates in the 74 ridings of Quebec in the months to come. For when Quebeckers speak out at the polls they will be speaking out against a party that has allowed Quebeckers to suffer an unemployment rate which is at times a full two percentage points above the national average.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right on. Shame.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They will speak out against a government that forces Quebeckers under the age of 25 to make their entry into the work force a particularly discouraging and difficult one.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, and I see the Minister of Transport smiling.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They will speak out against the type of price instability that makes maintaining a decent standard of living, let alone improving one's standard of living, a discouraging and impossible battle for Quebeckers of all ages.
My colleague for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) has already put forward the type of bold step a Stanfield government would have taken to move the economy of Quebec and of other provinces forward while ensuring that a basic form of price and cost stability was maintained. By comparison, the Turner budget lacks both imagination and understanding and deserves neither the trust nor support of the Canadian people.
February 28, 1973

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This budget, as the Minister of Finance said, strengthens and supplements the budget introduced in the House in May 1972. It is true, Mr. Speaker, in this sense that it strengthens and supplements the image the people of Canada had of the incompetence and the loss of credibility of this government in general and the Minister of Finance in particular.
The challenge, Mr. Speaker, was not to convince the New Democrats but all Canadians. For our part-and it is the challenge-we are ready to meet the real needs of all Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to enter this debate on the budget. The hon. member who last spoke quoted that great statesman and made the analogy that never have so many taken so long to do so little for those they represent. After listening to his speech, with all its colourful rhetoric and very few specifics, I think I can say that never have I heard so many people in the opposition talk so much and offer so little.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member talked about what the Turner budget has done for the young Quebecker. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Is he not aware of that fact? Is he not aware of the millions, indeed hundreds of millions of dollars which have gone to that province, as they have to other provinces, as our share in the cost of post-secondary education? Does he condemn the Opportunities for Youth program?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Let me remind him that there are many tariff cuts and sales tax cuts which are designed to increase the purchasing power

of the very housewives in Quebec about whom he speaks. Let me also remind the hon. member that it was this government which not so many months ago brought before this House a family income security plan.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who killed it?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Precisely. I wish the hon. member would keep interrupting; he is very helpful. I will tell him who killed it. Members of the official opposition killed it by delaying tactics throughout the debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Some members of the official opposition from Newfoundland-one or two are not here now because they did not survive the last election- will testify that the Conservative party's position on FISP was a positive embarrassment to them in that province. That bill would have redistributed an additional $180 million over and above the $650 million already in the program to those very children and families about which the hon. member spoke. The hon. member is now a front bencher of the party which did so much to destroy the legislation that would have greatly helped young families in the province of Quebec as well as in other provinces of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about jobs?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member asks about jobs. That shows how preposterous is the economic thinking on the other side, when they do not realize that an increase of this kind in social security moneys going to those in the lower income groups increases their disposable income and purchasing power for goods they desperately need and, by its very nature, creates jobs. Is that not what the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies) has been trying to tell us and his own party?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are the minister of unemployment, not employment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Maybe the hon. member who just spoke has one advantage. He is a new member. For obvious reasons, he has chosen not to take any responsibility whatsoever for the past conduct of the party he represents.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe spoke with passion about the high rate of unemployment in the province of Quebec but offered very few specifics to correct the situation in terms of policies. He was a member of the Conservative party which not so many days ago took a position that would have cut off moneys to the very unemployed he pretends to care about.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He speaks about his concern for families of Quebec. Let him justify the position of his party on the FISP bill that would have done so much for the children of his province. I do not think he can. I had an opportunity to read the speech of the hon. member for Don Valley. I read in the newspapers that the hon.

February 28, 1973
The Budget-Hon. John C. Munro member lor Don Valley is the new financial critic for the Conservative party. I looked forward with considerable anticipation to his speech. Knowing his background in the academic field, I thought we might find something there of a novel nature which would be constructive. I found not one original thought in that speech.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You should hear yourself.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope his students felt he made a better contribution to their benefit than members of this House felt he did to theirs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I doubt whether members of the government felt that way.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member who has just spoken referred to the great new formula which the hon. member for Don Valley had offered. But when you strip away the rhetoric, his solutions to unemployment and the economic problems confronting the country aside from policies already in place turned out to be wage and price controls. He talked about a 90-day period, a stabilization period, whatever that means; but I found an amazing lack of detail as to precisely what would happen after that period of 90 days.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Sixty days.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He talked about wage and price controls. Nowhere in his speech did I see any suggestion that there ought to be any type of control of profits. When we talk about wage and price controls and offer them as some solution to the economic ills of the country, I believe we should be careful not to raise expectations among the people who are suffering most from inflation and from unemployment-expectations which can never be fulfilled. I take it that the hon. member for Don Valley would be the very first to admit that in terms of the unemployment which we have been facing and which we have been trying to cure-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Unsuccessfully.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, come on!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -wage and price control is not a solution which will lower unemployment in the short term.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Try it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If he is suggesting that it will-and it would appear that his party is doing so by the line it is taking-he is misleading the Canadian people. The fact is that wage and price controls, unless one spells out specifically how they would work and to whom they would apply and whether they would apply to profits, all too often hurt the very people who can least afford to bear their weight. I refer to the people in the lower income groups. These are the ones earning wages and salaries.

These are the ones who could be subjected to control most effectively. These are the ones who enjoy the least benefits in terms of stock options, expense accounts, and so on, as a means of getting around controls. Any equitable approach to wage and price controls must ensure that the working population of this country is not asked to accept the full burden of such restrictions while those who enjoy profits, stock options and other sources of income escape.
The hon. member and other members of the Official Opposition talk about tax cuts. They suggest tax cuts across the board.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Right.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What novelty is there in that? Those in the higher income groups get the greatest benefit. That has been the traditional position of the Conservative party. I thought the hon. member for Don Valley would have something better to offer.
This budget places minimum and maximum limits on tax cuts so that they can exert maximum impact on the people who should benefit most-the people in the middle and lower income groups. Who would argue with that? This budget also increases real income by effecting reductions in sales tax. I think the hon. member for Don Valley would admit that, traditionally, sales taxes are retrogressive; they have been most severely felt by those in the lower income groups. By reducing sales taxes we are helping the people in the lower income groups who need help most. Surely, no one would disagree with that philosophy.
Mr. Speaker, we are considering a budget which increases disposable income, which reduces tariffs, which reduces sales tax, which reduces customs duties. Second, it reduces taxes. The hon. member for Don Valley has talked about this, but in a much less progressive fashion. The budget reduces taxes in a way which will have a major impact upon those who most need increased disposable income-the low income groups. Third, it contains a built-in mechanism as an inflationary hedge. It does so in a way which will work. I believe even the hon. member for Don Valley will admit that this type of inflationary hedge mechanism built into the platform of the Conservative party would have been entirely inoperative.
Fourth, it contains incentives to private industry to increase capitalization, modernize plants and upgrade technology, thereby improving the strength of its position in world markets. This is what hon. members opposite have been talking about during the question period. Fifth, it continues a policy of injecting money into the economy so as to provide jobs through such programs as Opportunities for Youth, LIP and manpower training. This provides a direct stimulus to the economy. Sixth, it increases disposable income in the hands of some 1,700,000 Canadians by expending many more hundreds of millions of dollars in this fiscal year on our senior citizens, one million of whom were surviving on all or part of the guaranteed income supplement. Now they will get a substantial increase in their pensions. Would anyone disagree that all these programs combine to increase substantially the amount of disposable income in the hands of Canadians?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a pleasure to be back in the House of Commons after an enforced absence. On the occasion of my first intervention in debate in this parliament, I would express my appreciation to the electors of the Fraser Valley East riding and publicly pledge my best efforts to represent them faithfully and effectively.
The current debate presents the opportunity to deal briefly with some of the issues facing us today, not only at the riding level but on a national scale, because we are well aware of the fact that the attitudes and actions of the national government establish the broad economic framework within which all Canadians must operate. In view of this fact, it can be readily understood that the altered stance of the government, as indicated in the last two budgets, cannot help but cause wonderment and confusion in the minds of the general public as to the direction in which this country is being led. The dilemma was clearly presented by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) on Friday last when he asked the question:
How can you trust a government that within the short space of a few months has accepted so much of what it previously rejected, and in turn has rejected so much of what just a few months ago it readily accepted?
As my riding includes a substantial part of the limited arable land of British Columbia, I would first make some observations with respect to what is termed rural Canada. Economically and socially, rural Canada is facing a crisis in 1973, and the policies of this government are doing little to remove the source of that crisis. These problems are caused mainly by the increasing loss of manpower to the cities. Economically, rural Canada suffers an over-all loss in net income that has intensified over the past four years. In 1951, for example, 37.05 per cent of Canada's population was rural. By 1961, the rural population was down to 30 per cent, and in 1971 to 23.6 per cent. The reason for this exodus to the cities is obvious when we realize that in 1969 a full 36 per cent of families living in rural areas lived below the Statistics Canada poverty line. For unattached persons in rural areas the percentage was 50.4 per cent.
As well, four out of every ten Canadian farmers find it necessary to be employed to some degree in a non-farm job. In most cases this extra income only brings them up to the poverty line. Little wonder, then, that many farmers have given up the land and have moved to the city to try
The Budget-Mr. Patterson
to make a living there. In a lot of cases these individuals do not have the skills necessary for employment in industry and therefore end up on the welfare rolls.
Agriculture in Canada, then, is still facing serious problems. One example is the decrease in realized net farm income. When we study these figures, we realize just how serious that problem has become. It is during this period of falling income that inflation and the cost of living have been the highest. It is the responsibility of the government to see that no individual is caught in the price squeeze- that income is, for all, adequate to purchase the necessities of life. I would submit that this government has failed in this responsibility, especially as it pertains to rural agricultural Canadians. Increased costs of production have certainly not been accompanied by increased prices for products.
There are one or two specific matters to which I should like to direct attention today, but because of the time factor I would just call the attention of hon. members to the speech made by my colleague, the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Danforth) yesterday in respect of one of the most serious situations referred to in the budget.
British Columbia is perhaps in the most vulnerable position of all the provinces of Canada in regard to agricultural tariffs, mainly because of its location. Immediately to the south lie the states of Washington and Idaho which together produce by far the heaviest volume of potatoes of any area in North America. In addition, Washington is a major producer of most common vegetables.
British Columbia has already felt the impact of the rapid expansion of production to the south, a prime example being the collapse of the market structure for strawberries for processing following the sudden upsurge of production in Mexico in 1970-71. The resulting flood of berries in the North American market drove both U.S. and B.C. prices far below the cost of production. At that time this labour-intensive sector of the industry provided a return of $6 million annually in this province.
In view of this experience, it becomes readily apparent that the fruit and vegetable industry in my province is deeply concerned about the possibility that its position, already demonstrably vulnerable to external pressures, will be severely undermined by these concessions in the form of tariff reductions. They are unilateral and, as a result, we lose all our bargaining position with foreign nations with respect to their tariffs. I would suggest that not only does the reduction in tariffs place our producers in a very vulnerable position, making it extremely difficult in many instances for them to carry on their operations, but it will also have tremendously detrimental effects on the employment picture in Canada, for we all know that the agricultural industry provides a great deal of employment.
With the exception of southern Ontario and the Prairies, about three-quarters of all farms in Canada are considered small farms, according to the Statistics Canada census, 1966, and it is these small farmers who bear the brunt of the inept agricultural policies of this government. I believe this is what concerns a great many of us today. The big man can take care of himself, but the little man

February 28, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Patterson
gets trampled by not only the big man but the big government, big taxes, big inflation and a bigger cost of living.
It is the same in the business world. Figures compiled by Dun and Bradstreet of Canada Ltd. last fall show that Canadian business failures during August, 1972, were the highest for that month since the depression years. They rose a fantastic 61 per cent since 1971, from 145 business failures to 233. These figures show that the ailment was widespread and general, for by region there were more failures in August, 1972, than a year earlier in every province except Saskatchewan, while Toronto led the nation with more than twice the number recorded in 1971.
There should be no reason for puzzlement about the rise in business failure and the drastic loss in productivity. Since the beginning of last year the Economic Council of Canada, along with my leader, warned that a healthy economy would require giving far more purchasing power and initiative back to the small businessman. Yet this government, this finance minister both in the budget he presented last May and in the one he presented last Monday night has to all intents and purposes ignored the plight of small business in this country.
We all know that attempts at tax reform led big government to ignore the vital interests of small business, yet small business in this country generates more employment, more real growth, more tax revenue and bears more of the cost burden of government than does so-called big business. It is my position and the position of this party that provision should be made for Canadian citizens to invest in the equity of Canadian-owned small business. We believe that the credit, which will be 50 per cent of qualified investments to a maximum of $5,000 each year, will either be offset against the person's income tax or rebated directly to him. This means that a Canadian who invests, for example, $1,000 in a qualified business or company will receive a credit of $500 against his income.
If implemented, the cost of such a program would be about $300 million-"cost" in the sense that this would be lost to federal revenue and treated as deferred personal tax. It would, however, be far less than the $1 billion spent on unemployment insurance payments to sustain an unemployment rate of 7 per cent. I realize that this government does not learn lessons very easily or very quickly, but surely by now it has learned that if we want to create jobs and encourage enterprise, the least effective way to do it is by direct government spending. As has been so clearly stated in this debate, the budget does virtually nothing to assist small businesses nor to encourage investment in small Canadian-owned enterprises.
The mention of tax reform brings to mind the introduction of a bill to introduce a great new deal for the Canadian taxpayers but in fact was, I believe, the perpetration of one of the greatest hoaxes by the Liberal government. It was a massive document, so complex that not even its authors were able to adequately explain either its intricacies or its ramifications. Rammed through parliament with indecent haste and characteristic Liberal arrogance, it further aggravated an already unintelligible jungle of tax laws and regulations.
A further move of the present government was the introduction of a new set of income tax forms that in their
effect add insult to injury and have caused consternation in the minds of taxpayers across the nation. An advertisement in one of the west coast newspapers vividly portrayed the situation when it called attention to the fact that in view of the new tax forms there would be a tremendous demand for the services of tax consultants, and offered courses to prepare for this lucrative development. Accountants time and time again have complained that answers to inquiries cannot be obtained at the taxation offices of the Department of National Revenue. The magnitude of the muddle caused by the tax measure and tax forms is eclipsed only by the confused and confusing picture drawn either deliberately or unintentionally by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in the presentation of the budget currently before the House.
We appreciate the announced reductions in personal income taxes, but without an effective program to halt the constantly increasing cost of living, Canadians could well find that through the further erosion of the value of the dollar all benefits accruing from tax reductions will be effectively wiped out. We have constantly urged the elimination of the 11 per cent tax on building materials. I firmly believe this would be a practical and effective way to encourage the building of new homes. The exorbitantly high interest rates should be reduced and the interest paid on mortgage payments should be deductible for income tax purposes, as should the municipal taxes on property. We continue to advance these proposals as deserving of the consideration of government.
May I also raise another matter to which attention has been called on many occasions; that is, the desirability of the government facing up to the unfairness of the situation and settling in an equitable manner the pleas of the original purchasers of Government of Canada 3 per cent perpetual bonds sold, I believe, in 1936. There are a limited number of individuals involved and I believe the source of hardship and resentment should be eliminated by a settlement of the issue.
The government's policy with regard to inflation was even more disastrous than its agricultural and small business policy. I would remind the House of what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in 1969 about his government's policy toward inflation. He said, on December 22, 1969, about what he termed our worst enemy, inflation:
There are a lot of people in this country who are bargaining that, oh well, the government can't hang tough for too long because it will only get frightened when it sees unemployment go up to 6 per cent. But if people think we are going to lose our nerve now, they should think again. We're not.
I think this is a shameful thing for the Prime Minister to say. If we look at the social and economic costs of the unemployment we have suffered, they would seem to indicate that there have been incalculable losses to the Canadian people, and this in the midst of statements by the Minister of Finance telling the poor people of the country that it was perfectly possible for a Canadian family to get along on $30 a week. If the government's policy to fight inflation had worked, then perhaps the Canadian people could forgive it for the chaos it brought about in the economic system. But the fact is that it did

February 28, 1973

not work and we still have inflation and high unemployment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to take part in this debate. We have heard from one Liberal, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), we have heard from a recycled Grit, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) who has returned after having dwelt in the political wilderness of Quebec, and we have heard from the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson), a recycled Social Crediter who failed to mention the Bank of Canada. So the debate this afternoon has been close to being interesting.
I wish to deal with a number of matters. I note that with great piousness the government introduced a 5 per cent reduction in personal income tax in such a manner that the individual taxpayer will receive a reduction of a minimum of $100 or a maximum of $500; this will apply to the middle and lower income people in this country. I point out to the minister that it was this government, while it had a majority, which brought in a 3 per cent reduction in income tax in respect of which the greatest benefit went to those in the upper income group and not to those in the middle or lower income groups. Because of the development of a minority government in this parliament, the government has had to change its position and bring in this budget.
I believe there are things in the budget which will be of benefit, I hope, at least to the consumers of the constituency of Assiniboia. It is on that basis and with some reluctance that I support the budget. I want to point out that the government has increased the old age pension to $100 and the supplement to $170. I say to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), who is present, that in terms of the real needs of the pensioners in this country that kind of increase is not good enough and the government must look toward a greater increase. In addition, there is the matter of the age limit being lowered from 65 to 60. This is a question with which we must deal in the near future. Many widows and widowers between age 60 and age 65 have real need and very limited sources of income. A drop in the age level for eligibility in respect of pensions is greatly needed. I do, however, accept the increases in the sense of meeting the need as of April 1, 1973. I shall continue to push for a further increase across the board to $150 a month which is advocated by the New Democratic Party.
I might mention the manner in which the income tax reduction of 5 per cent with a maximum of $500 and a minimum of $100 was brought in. That is a plank which was stolen from the platform of the New Democratic Party. I say to hon. members that they can steal these planks all they like, so long as it is done for the people of Canada and so long as the greatest benefit goes to the people in the middle and lower income brackets. On top of that, we have seen the raising of the exemptions which I spoke about in my constituency during the election.
The Budget-Mr. Knight
These exemptions have been increased for the ordinary taxpayers of Canada.
Further, we have seen a reduction in tariffs. There is a temporary reduction involving in the neighbourhood of $1.3 billion worth of goods. I point out to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) that the significance of this reduction in tariffs is that it establishes a precedent in the area of tariff-setting in this country. For the first time in a long while a government has moved in the area of reducing tariffs on certain commodities. This may or may not benefit the consumer of this country, but a precedent has been set which those of us from the west will watch with great interest, no matter which old-line party is in power. People in the west have lived for a long time under the protective umbrella of tariffs which did nothing but protect the interests of the people in the east. So a very important precedent has been set in terms of the future development of the country.
Because this government is in a minority position we have had a reduction in sales tax on such things as children's clothing, shoes and other footwear. That is significant. I have already had managers of stores and co-operatives writing me for further details in order to lower the price of their products. If this reduction is passed on to the consumer, it will help to lower the cost of living, especially for people who are at present raising children and are in need of all the purchasing power they can get.
Furthermore, there is in this budget an equalization formula which increases payments by some $190 million to the Maritimes, the Atlantic provinces, Quebec, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. This will be of further assistance in giving purchasing power to people in Saskatchewan where we are attempting to alleviate the pressure of the property tax, to shift it more in relation to a man's income. We are trying to reduce school property tax as a cost. That is important in terms of what is in the budget, coming from a minority government.
Further to that, there has been some change in the area of tax reform. I will not jump with joy over a couple of these changes, for a number of reasons. When the minister made his speech in the House of Commons, he mentioned that the capital gains tax has been removed from the transfer of a farm from father to son, so as to keep the farm units going. The Minister of Agriculture jumped with great glee at that and shook the hand of the Minister of Finance, praising him to his colleagues around him, I am sure. Then he probably went home that night and made the mistake of reading the details and finding out that first you had to drop dead before getting this exemption.
We in this party moved an amendment against the tax reform bill of 1971 to exempt the transfer of farmland which kept the farm unit going from father to son or even daughter-in-law. We moved that amendment, but the government has not gone far enough and the Minister of Agriculture, for all his talk, should not get so excited about it. I am sure there are other things in the budget that did not excite the Minister of Agriculture. There has been a move back to allowing a producer to set up a basic herd. That is important in my area for many people
1768

February 28, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Knight
involved in the cattle industry. This is a move in the right direction, although it does not go far enough in setting up basic herds. These are the things in the budget that have some merit.
We have now left the kind of dinosaur economic philosophy which was practised in 1969, 1970 and 1971 and are moving in the direction of an expansionary budget, although it does not go far enough. We are moving in this direction only because this is a minority government, and as insensitive as it has been during its four years of governing, the government now finds itself in a minority situation and reacts thereto.
I suppose that when we reach 5.45 p.m. tonight and we get to the point of voting on the final element of this budget, we will find the Tory party voting against the following measures. It will vote against an increase in the old age pension. It will vote against an increase in war veterans allowances. It will vote against the reduction of 5 per cent in personal income tax with a maximum of $500 and a minimum of $100. It will vote against the removal of the tax on children's clothing, etc. This budget provision will be of great value to the young consumers in my constituency.
Tory members from the Maritimes, Saskatchewan and Manitoba will be voting against the equalization formula in order to provide additional moneys amounting to $190 million to the revenue of those provincial governments, to assist in the education and property tax. That is what they will do at 5.45 p.m. They will vote against a change in the capital gains tax as it relates to farmers, limited as it is. They will vote against the change in the basic herd concept, limited as that change is. This should be on the record, Mr. Speaker.
In the few moments that I have left I want to say that this government which bases its philosophy on outdated concepts, as outdated as those of the party to my right, has not yet begun to deal with the real issues; and this budget does not deal with the real issues that face the people of this country, such as the redistribution of income. Although there is a limited redistribution of income in this budget, it has not been carried out in terms of a fundamental change in the tax system, in spite of the cries of some members of the Tory party that the system is unfair to their big business friends.
Further to that, there is a need to revamp our housing programs. There is real need for a strong foreign takeover bill, stronger than the one presented to this parliament, to meet the real challenge of the continual increase in the foreign ownership of our economy. One issue that will tickle the hearts and the fancies of the members of the Tory party is the energy policy. We are facing an energy crisis, and let there be no mistake about it, in spite of the cry from the Tory members from Alberta and in spite of the weak-kneed approach to the whole issue by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald). The government's energy policy is a disaster. It is a disaster when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the National Energy Board come before the committee of the House and state that on the night of February 1 they did not know whether they had enough oil resourdes for the month of February.

Since one of the Tory members from Alberta is trying to speak up, let me remind him that the Tory members present in the committee said that there is no problem, no crisis; we do not need any quotas or controls, everything is fine, let us export in the traditional free enterprise system. One of the Tory members from Calgary pointed out in the committee a fundamental issue facing the people of this country, that is, the price that we will have to pay for our natural resources if we keep selling our present reserves. We will then have to rely on the reserves in the Mackenzie delta and in the Arctic. If we keep selling them, the consumers in my constituency, because of the free enterprise philosophy of that party in Alberta and of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, will be paying twice as much for their fuel requirements. This is what my constituents will have to do; and this applies to the farmer, the consumer of natural gas in the city, the old age pensioner and everybody else.
What this country needs is a fundamental policy related to the redistribution of income, related to housing, to control of foreign ownership, and above all in this decade we need a national energy policy to answer the real needs of the Canadian consumer.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on the optimism he has shown in the "Budget Highlights" which he handed out to hon. members on Monday, February 19, 1973.
In this publication, the first words of the Minister of Finance are as follows:
A budget designed to reduce unemployment and to stimulate a more rapid growth
If, as stated by the Minister of Finance, this is the first goal of his department and of the government on the fight against unemployment, we shall be the first to support him as long as the legislation proposed by the government is really adequate.
As the NDP spokesmen said, that party is naturally inclined to support the government as well as the budget of the Minister of Finance where the government states its intention of fighting unemployment.
As to hon. members of the official opposition, I think their feelings have been expressed by their financial critic, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) who told the House on February 21:
Coming to the point of unemployment and those massive measures needed to turn the corner, Mr. Speaker, all sorts of proposals have been tried by the government over the past several years but there were still 688,000 people seeking work this last month.
The hon. member for Edmonton West has good cause for being shocked because 688,000 persons had no paid job last January. Members of the official Opposition are undoubtedly right when they state that the measures proposed in the past and still being proposed by the government to combat unemployment will not have the expected results.
February 28, 1973

The Canadian people are justified in distrusting a government which, at a time when all kinds of goods are plentiful, allow so many people to live in destitution.
Mr. Speaker, one may wonder whether the Progressive Conservatives could do better. Have they found practical ways to cope with the unemployment problem? What were their solutions when they were in office from 1958 to 1962? Do they have better answers to offer now and what concrete measures to they suggest?
We of the Social Credit Party of Canada would like it very much if the Progressive Conservatives could suggest solutions likely to solve the unemployment problem. We would like to be able to endorse all their criticisms about the present situation and we would like very much to see another government at the head of the country.
Unfortunately, the Progressive Conservatives who offer themselves as alternative solutions to the Liberals have no credibility when it comes to fighting against unemployment. They have no credibility and they will not have the chance, I think, to replace the present government because electors aware that the Progressive Conservatives have no solution to offer to settle the unemployment issue. They have shown their inefficacy and their ineffectiveness when they were in power in Canada from 1958 to 1962.
In September 1971, Statistics Canada published a most interesting and revealing study on the unemployment problem in Canada. Entitled "Unemployment Data, 196071" this study enables us to analyse the unemployment situation in the course of the years 1960, 1965 and 1970.
Here are the yearly average unemployment rates in relation to the total manpower for each of the five Canadian areas. For the Atlantic region, in 1970, the unemployment rate amounted to 7.6 per cent in relation to the total manpower; in 1965, it was 7.4 per cent, and in 1960, under the Progressive Conservative government, the unemployment rate reached 10.7 per cent.
For the Quebec region, in 1970, the rate of unemployment stood at 7.9 per cent; in 1965, 5.4 per cent, and in 1960, 9.1 per cent, which means that in Quebec also, the rate of unemployment was higher under the Progressive Conservative regime of the sixties.
In Ontario, we note the same occurrence: the unemployment rate was 4.3 per cent in 1970 and 5.4 per cent in 1960.
In the Prairies, unemployment reached 4.4 per cent in 1970 and 4.2 per cent in 1960.
Lastly, in British Columbia, the unemployment rate was 7.6 per cent in 1970 and 8.5 per cent in 1960, under the Progressive Conservative government.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that with such a record and so poor a performance in respect of unemployment, the Progressive Conservatives have nothing to teach anyone and they should be the least inclined to criticize the present government which has not been and is not able to check unemployment.
According to statistical data from January 1953 to December 1971, here is the unemployment situation from 1959 to 1962, under the Progressive Conservative government, and from 1968 to 1971, under the Liberal government.
The Budget-Mr. Godin
In 1959, the unemployment rate, by sex and age categories, was 6 per cent. It roses to 7 per cent in 1960. It reached 7.1 per cent in 1961, decreasing to 5.9 per cent in 1962, when the Progressive Conservative party was in office.
In 1968, under the government of the present right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the unemployment rate was 4.8 per cent; it fell to 4.7 per cent in 1969 and again went up to 5.9 per cent in 1970, reaching 6.4 per cent in
1971.
On pages 12 and 141 of Catalogue 71-201 showing unemployment and labour figures from January 1953 to December 1971, there is clear evidence that the unemployment rate, from 1958 to 1962, under a Progressive Conservative government, reached absolute figures higher than those registered under this government from 1968 to 1971.
Mr. Speaker, I would not take the time of the House to quote all the figures available to me, but may I say only that in 1961 the labour force had 2 million fewer workers than in 1971. The unemployment figure reached 716,000 in February 1961 and 702,000 in March 1961.
Under this government, the unemployment figure never exceeded 700,000, although in Canada the labour force has increased by two million workers.
Therefore, the unemployment rate stood at 11.4 per cent in March 1961, 11.24 per cent in February 1961 and 10.77 per cent in January 1961.
An analysis of these statistical data enlightens us on how the Progressive Conservative party members felt about the problem of unemployment when they occupied the front benches. I therefore cannot bring myself to place confidence in the Progressive Conservatives when they are dealing with this problem because they did worse than the present government when they were in power.
It is true that the Progressive Conservatives have changed their leader since 1962 but I believe, that the party's past record has not been impressive. We even have some documents to the effect that the present leader (Mr. Stanfield) has never been very popular. The people of Canada cannot even grant him the benefit of the doubt, saying "Let us gives him a chance to prove himself, since he has already been tested as premier of Nova Scotian".
As a matter in fact, in issue No. 39, for March 21, 1967, of the proceedings of the Joint Senate and Commons Committee on Consumer Credit, we find a brief submitted by Mr. Duncan MacIntyre, who represented a department of St. Francis Xavier University as well as low-income families of the eastern ridings of the province. Now, the author of this brief states that only three constituencies in the province had less than 40 per cent poor families. In fact, in some constituencies, 59, 56, and even 63 per cent of families were poor.
If one uses the same criteria as were used in writing the brief, one can say the Mr. MacIntyre was perfectly right, since the families he refers to were, and I quote:
(1)	families other than agricultural families, with incomes under $3,000;
(2)	agricultural families with incomes under $2,500;
25789-40)

February 28, 1973
The Budget-Mr. Godin
Using these figures, constituencies could be found in Nova Scotia where 63 per cent of families were not even getting the wretched incomes mentioned above.
Since, therefore, we cannot trust the solutions put forward by the Liberals, because they have not put an end to unemployment or prevented prices from rising, and since we cannot trust in the Progressive Conservatives, because they were no more successful in bringing prosperity and security to Canadians from 1958 to 1962, I suggest that all that remains to us is to try Social Credit, which has not yet failed us and is full of promises.
I imagine that the majority of hon. members are not happy about the misery and distress of almost 700,000 Canadians who have no jobs in this country. So we, of the Social Credit Party of Canada, want to ensure economic freedom and security for all Canadians. For this, we propose that the Canadian population apply a system which has never been applied anywhere, and which cannot be worse than the one proposed in turn by the Liberals and the Progressive Conservatives.
It was on June 26, 1937, during a lecture he gave in London, that the founder of Social Credit gave a detailed definition of it. Here it is:
In the minds of many people, Social Credit is a plan for monetary reform, and that is why today when money and credit are scarce the monetary reforms it proposes are so popular. But Social Credit is not only that, Social Credit is the policy of a philosophy. This philosophy may be described as the partnership philosophy or the power of human beings living in partnership to get the wanted results in order to meet their needs.
If we make a more thorough analysis, we may ask ourselves: What is credit? This is the answer: Credit is just the belief that partnership brings along benefits. For instance, the first Canadians relied on the wealth which were within their reach and able to meet their needs. That is what is called the real credit of a country. This credit includes the country's wealth as well as all the men who want to exploit them. Therefrom one may conclude, that the real credit of a country is a social common thing. Therefore, the real credit or the social credit is a reality, a fact for our country. But, if social credit is a reality, a fact, why do members of the Social Credit party not stop complaining, asking above all for social credit, trying to change the monetary system and to have enough members elected in Parliament in order to reach their objective? The only reason is, Mr. Speaker, that the present financial system does not reflect reality and that our bank system prevents consumers from taking advantage of the result of their partnership, because the financial system keeps for itself the benefits of partnership which should normally belong to every citizen.
This is the situation, Mr. Speaker, which led the Right Hon. Mackenzie King to say once, and I quote:
Yesterday's promises are today's taxes.
So that Canadians really benefit from the results of their partnership, we must therefore relate the financial credit to the real or social credit, that is to say relate money and credit to what Canadians produce and provide and are able to produce and provide.

Values that were far sounder and far more basic than the present bank system have been put aside. Religion, Catholicism, papal authority, private property, respect for the human life of the foetus, and many other things have been put aside.
And, Mr. Speaker, what about the desperation of international bankers who are seeking a new international bank system. If the international financial system has to be reconsidered and worked out again from scratch, this is because the national financial systems also have to be reconsidered and worked out again from scratch.
This, Mr. Speaker, is the task which the Creditistes are trying to carry out, being precursors and innovators, misunderstood perhaps and rejected sometimes because they dare attack finance. Fortunately, finance is no longer a taboo subject today, the monetary system is no longer sacro-sanct, and because facts prove us right, Creditistes are going to continue even more successfully, I think, to expose the present system which has no justification in the nature of things and perpetuates a false concept of money in a human society.
